description: Somos un equipo de ASIMET enfocado en la minería, el medio ambiente y la tecnología. Buscamos desarrollar soluciones innovadoras a desafíos globales mediante la ciencia, la creatividad y el uso de datos abiertos, contribuyendo al desarrollo sostenible.
summary: Space content for students often hides the real engineering trade-offs behind a mission, or explains them in a way that is too technical. Asimetitos is a free web game in which students build their own satellite, launch it and find out whether their mission succeeds. They pick a mission (a CubeSat, an Earth observer, a space telescope, a lunar orbiter or a Mars orbiter) and build the spacecraft from just four pieces: a science instrument, power, an antenna and a rocket, each in a small, medium or large size. Four simple bars (weight, power, money and science) react to every choice, and a GO / NO-GO "mission control" check explains in plain words what is wrong, so students discover that the biggest option is rarely the best one. A short simulated mission with random events shows why missions succeed or fail, and the result screen gives 0 to 3 stars, tips to improve and the real NASA mission their design resembles. It runs offline in a single HTML file and needs no account.
details:
What it does. The game has four simple steps:

1.     Choose a mission in a 3D carousel and a difficulty level.

2.     Build the spacecraft in a one-screen workshop: pick a small, medium or large option for each of the four pieces (science instrument, power, antenna, rocket) while a rotatable 3D model of the satellite assembles itself.

3.     Launch: when mission control says GO, watch the countdown, the launch and the mission in orbit, with random events such as solar storms or a lost ground station.

4.     Get the result: 0 to 3 stars, what went well, what to try next time and the real NASA mission the design resembles.

How it works. Behind the four pieces there is a simplified engineering model. Each option maps to real component types, and the rest of the spacecraft (structure, orbit, computer, attitude control, propulsion, thermal control) is chosen automatically for the mission. The model recalculates the whole mission after every choice:

•      Kepler's orbital period;

•      eclipse fraction from orbit geometry;

•      solar power and battery sizing;

•      downlink data volume from contact time;

•      propellant with the rocket equation;

•      cost with integration and operations;

•      lifetime and reliability with redundancy.

The four bars turn green, yellow or red, the mission-control check translates engineering problems into plain words (for example, "your spacecraft is too heavy for this rocket"), and every formula can be opened under "How is it calculated?". The mission simulation uses a seeded random generator with events such as solar storms, micrometeoroids or ground-station loss; good designs resist them. After each mission the game tests the alternatives and suggests the single piece change that would earn the most points.

Benefits.

•      Students experience real trade-offs in a few minutes: weight vs. power vs. money vs. science.

•      Only 4 decisions with 3 options each: simple enough for young students, but with 81 possible designs per mission.

•      Failing is part of learning: small parts sometimes do not work (a small antenna cannot reach Mars), and the game explains why.

•      They learn vocabulary through a built-in glossary and connect their design to real NASA missions.

•      Three difficulty levels; the expert level adds a tighter budget and a 15 % engineering margin.

Tools. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no libraries and no external assets:

•      the 3D spacecraft, carousel and orbit views are drawn in code (CSS 3D and Canvas 2D);

•      the sounds are synthesized with the Web Audio API;

•      it works offline, keeps no personal data and can be used with the keyboard and with reduced motion.

Creativity.

•      A 3D spacecraft that assembles piece by piece and can be rotated.

•      Floating 3D missions and difficulty levels (a green planet, a ringed planet and a black hole).

•      An animated launch sequence and a 3D orbit view showing eclipses and ground-station contacts.

A 0–3 star result with confetti and a comparison to a real mission.
